memory_candidates.content: When a shared, cross-theory framework routine (e.g. model_checker/iterate/models.py's build_new_model_structure) calls a theory-specific method (semantics.is_world(state)) unconditionally rather than behind a hasattr() guard -- unlike its own neighboring calls to other optional theory methods in the same function, which ARE guarded -- removing that theory's state-existence predicate as part of a semantic redesign will make the framework's iteration path crash outright (AttributeError) the first time a caller requests more than one model, rather than degrading gracefully. This kind of asymmetric guarding (some optional-method calls guarded, one sibling call in the same function not) is easy to miss during a redesign's own test suite if no existing test exercises iterate: N > 1 for that theory, since the default N=1 short-circuits before the unguarded code path is ever reached. Direct empirical testing (e.g. a real dev_cli.py run with iterate: 3 set) surfaces this kind of gap when code review alone does not.

A theory-wide pytest marker blanket applied by a pytest_collection_modifyitems hook (used here to quarantine an incomplete theory from release gating) can leave residual coupling in unexpected places once the underlying incompleteness is resolved: per-test markings outside the theory's own tree (an authorized allowlist for completeness claims coupled to the theory's solve cost), a dedicated CI contract test asserting the blanket's exact coverage, and prose in multiple documentation files all need updating together when the marker retires, not just the registration and the gating -m expressions. A repo-wide grep for the marker's own name (not just its registration site) is the reliable way to find every real consumer before declaring the retirement complete.
